analysis.one_liner: Bans the nerve-agent pesticide chlorpyrifos from food, farm fields, and export.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Chlorpyrifos is an organophosphate insecticide — a class of chemicals originally developed as nerve agents in World War II. The bill would make it illegal for food to contain any chlorpyrifos residue, would order the EPA to cancel the pesticide's registration, and would close the loophole that lets companies sell banned pesticides to other countries. It would also block the EPA from granting emergency exemptions that allow continued use.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, farmworkers, and rural families. The EPA's own 2016 risk assessment found that food residues expose children ages 1 to 2 to roughly 140 times the level the agency considers acceptable, that farmworkers who mix and apply the pesticide are exposed to unsafe levels even with maximum protective equipment, and that drinking water in agricultural communities exceeds safety limits [S3]. Prenatal exposure is associated with reduced IQ, memory loss, motor delays, and attention deficits in children [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes any food containing chlorpyrifos residue illegal, ending dietary exposure for everyone, with EPA data showing toddlers currently exposed at 140 times the acceptable level [S2] [S3].
Orders the EPA to cancel chlorpyrifos registrations outright and forbids new ones, removing the agency's discretion to keep it on the market despite its 2015 proposal to ban all food uses [S2] [S3].
Protects farmworkers, whom the EPA says face unsafe exposure even wearing maximum protective equipment, with unsafe levels persisting in fields for about 18 days after spraying [S3].
Prohibits exporting chlorpyrifos pesticides to other countries and blocks emergency exemptions that would otherwise let federal and state agencies keep using it [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers lose a product they have sold since 1965, and growers of apples, broccoli, onions, walnuts, cauliflower, corn, alfalfa, and other crops lose a widely used pest-control tool and would need substitutes or alternative practices [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and growers who use it

drawbacks.text: Growers relied on chlorpyrifos on a wide range of crops — more than half of the nation's apple and broccoli crops between 2006 and 2012 — and an immediate ban would force them to find and pay for alternatives, with some cost likely passed to consumers [S3].

The bill removes the EPA's case-by-case discretion entirely, canceling registrations without the usual notice-and-comment process and without allowing economic benefits to be weighed against the health standard, which is a legitimate design objection for opponents [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health evidence in the record is one-sided: the EPA itself concluded in 2016 that no use of chlorpyrifos on food meets the legal safety standard, that children's exposures vastly exceed acceptable levels, and that farmworkers cannot be protected even with full gear [S3]. The costs fall on a concentrated set of manufacturers and on growers who would need substitute products, while the benefit is reduced neurodevelopmental harm to children and poisonings among farmworkers. The bill is a blunt instrument, but the underlying safety finding it acts on came from the regulator's own risk assessment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it died there in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the bill on March 28, 2019, joined by 13 original Senate cosponsors including Booker, Sanders, Harris, and Markey [S1] [S3].
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill in total — 15 Democrats and 1 independent — with no Republican support [S4].

The Senate referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].

The bill's findings section notes that in August 2018 the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ordered the EPA to move forward with a chlorpyrifos ban, and that the EPA appealed the ruling rather than comply [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chlorpyrifos manufacturers and the growers who used it are better off, since the pesticide stayed on the market; farmworkers, children in agricultural communities, and food consumers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over pesticide law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Trump administration EPA
against.what_they_did: Kept chlorpyrifos on the market despite its own 2015 proposal to ban all food uses, and appealed the Ninth Circuit's order to ban it rather than comply.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders, and no Republican signed on; the Republican-run Agriculture Committee was where the bill stalled with no action.

industries.note: Chlorpyrifos, first registered in 1965, would be banned outright and could no longer be sold domestically or exported abroad. The industry's interest in keeping the product on the market ran directly against the EPA's own safety findings.

Growers of apples, broccoli, onions, walnuts, cauliflower, corn, and alfalfa used chlorpyrifos heavily and would lose an effective, inexpensive insecticide. Their preference to keep using it conflicted with reducing pesticide exposure for farmworkers and rural families.
